headline: AI on Android may access your sensitive data, even if encrypted
summary: While on-device processing promises privacy, companies can update software to send data to servers. End-to-end encryption doesn't protect data once decrypted by AI.
details: AI on Android devices is becoming increasingly integrated, with Google Assistant and Gemini embedded deeply into the operating system. While the industry touts on-device processing as a privacy safeguard, this isn't always a permanent guarantee. Companies can update their software to process data remotely, potentially compromising user privacy.

Even with end-to-end encryption (E2EE) on apps, AI screen-reading capabilities can access data once it's decrypted and displayed as plain text on your device. This means sensitive information, like passwords or financial details, could be exposed.

Examples like Microsoft's controversial Recall feature highlight the risks. It captured screenshots indiscriminately, including private messages and banking information, before being made opt-in after public backlash.

Anthropic's Claude Mythos Preview was deemed too dangerous for release due to cybersecurity risks, yet Amazon demonstrated how vulnerabilities could be exploited. Similarly, Google's Gemini has documented permissions to access call logs, contacts, and message history.

A vulnerability called GeminiJack demonstrated how malicious inputs could trick Gemini into stealing data. While Google patched this, the AI's continued access to sensitive information, even with activity settings off, remains a concern.

Furthermore, some AI providers reserve the right to use user data, including screen content and prompts, to improve their models. This means your unpublished work or confidential business information could inadvertently train future AI systems.
caption:
Giving AI constant background access to your Android screen might be a privacy nightmare. Here's why.

AI on Android devices is becoming increasingly integrated, with Google Assistant and Gemini embedded deeply into the operating system. While the industry touts on-device processing as a privacy safeguard, this isn't always a permanent guarantee. Companies can update their software to process data remotely, potentially compromising user privacy.

Even with end-to-end encryption (E2EE) on apps, AI screen-reading capabilities can access data once it's decrypted and displayed as plain text on your device. This means sensitive information, like passwords or financial details, could be exposed.

Examples like Microsoft's controversial Recall feature highlight the risks. It captured screenshots indiscriminately, including private messages and banking information, before being made opt-in after public backlash.

Anthropic's Claude Mythos Preview was deemed too dangerous for release due to cybersecurity risks, yet Amazon demonstrated how vulnerabilities could be exploited. Similarly, Google's Gemini has documented permissions to access call logs, contacts, and message history.

A vulnerability called GeminiJack demonstrated how malicious inputs could trick Gemini into stealing data. While Google patched this, the AI's continued access to sensitive information, even with activity settings off, remains a concern.

Furthermore, some AI providers reserve the right to use user data, including screen content and prompts, to improve their models. This means your unpublished work or confidential business information could inadvertently train future AI systems.

Source: Android Police

headline_marked: [[The Seinfeld Chronicles]] Digital Edition Explores Sitcom's Creative Process
headline: The Seinfeld Chronicles Digital Edition Explores Sitcom's Creative Process
summary: A data-driven exploration of every Seinfeld episode, originally published as a limited-edition book, is now being revisited for a wider audience.
details: The beloved sitcom Seinfeld, known for its unique deviation from traditional storytelling with its faster-paced multi-story structure and focus on everyday minutiae, has inspired a deep dive into its creative process.
This self-motivated, data-driven exploration began as a way to understand how creators Jerry Seinfeld and Larry David, along with their writing team, achieved sustained brilliance.
The initial product of this extensive analysis was 'The Seinfeld Chronicles,' a limited-edition printed book released in 2020, with 176 copies matching the number of written episodes.
This book reached a small but passionate audience, but the creator felt it was time to revisit the work and develop a new format to reach a wider audience.

The project aims to visually explore the sitcom through its data, akin to a sports coach assembling the right players to win a game, this project seeks to understand how the Seinfeld 'coaching team' used their resources to assemble characters and scenes for maximum comedic effect.
The title 'The Seinfeld Chronicles' itself refers to the pilot episode of the show, originally known as 'Good News, Bad News,' or 'Pilot'.
caption:
Seinfeld, the show about nothing, is getting the ultimate data-driven deep dive.

The beloved sitcom Seinfeld, known for its unique deviation from traditional storytelling with its faster-paced multi-story structure and focus on everyday minutiae, has inspired a deep dive into its creative process.

This self-motivated, data-driven exploration began as a way to understand how creators Jerry Seinfeld and Larry David, along with their writing team, achieved sustained brilliance.

The initial product of this extensive analysis was 'The Seinfeld Chronicles,' a limited-edition printed book released in 2020, with 176 copies matching the number of written episodes.

This book reached a small but passionate audience, but the creator felt it was time to revisit the work and develop a new format to reach a wider audience.

The project aims to visually explore the sitcom through its data, akin to a sports coach assembling the right players to win a game, this project seeks to understand how the Seinfeld 'coaching team' used their resources to assemble characters and scenes for maximum comedic effect.

The title 'The Seinfeld Chronicles' itself refers to the pilot episode of the show, originally known as 'Good News, Bad News,' or 'Pilot'.

#Seinfeld #Sitcom #DataAnalysis #TVHistory #Comedy

Source: Hacker News
